as_told.title: 1950s press reports that aircraft firms had cracked anti-gravity

plain: This story is about a set of newspaper articles from the 1950s saying that big American aircraft companies had suddenly become interested in anti-gravity, meaning ways to fly by cancelling or controlling gravity instead of using engines or wings. A physicist named Hal Puthoff, speaking on a podcast hosted by Jesse Michels, says a writer named Talbert wrote the series, and that it ran in the Miami Herald and other papers. Puthoff says Talbert found that a number of aerospace engineering firms were chasing the idea, and he mentions the physicist Bryce DeWitt in connection with it. A philosopher named Jason Jorjani tells it too, on the same podcast. He does not name Talbert, but says the articles quoted the chairmen of the aircraft makers Martin, Lear and Convair, and that the firms had cracked anti-gravity. He points to a book called Closer Encounters as his source. If true, it would mean serious work on new ways of flying was under way, and then went quiet, decades ago.
